title: Resistivity in Dilute Cu-3d Alloys Governed by Disorder-Induced Band Broadening
abstract: The mechanism governing the resistivity in dilute Cu-3d transition-metal alloys at ambient temperature -- the regime relevant to most practical applications and distinct from the low-temperature, Kondo-screened regime addressed by earlier theoretical work -- is investigated using first-principles calculations based on the Korringa--Kohn--Rostoker coherent potential approximation combined with the Kubo--Greenwood formalism. The paramagnetic state is described within the disordered local moment (DLM) framework, corresponding to a local-moment paramagnet rather than a Pauli paramagnet. We show that the experimentally observed resistivity trends are reproduced only within the DLM description, while nonmagnetic and ferromagnetic states fail to capture the correct element dependence. Contrary to conventional interpretations based on the density of states at the Fermi level, the resistivity exhibits a strong correlation with the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the Bloch spectral function (BSF) on the Fermi surface. This correlation reflects the disorder-induced lifetime broadening of electronic states, directly related to the scattering rate that governs electrical resistivity. A common power-law scaling between resistivity and BSF broadening is identified across different magnetic states. These results demonstrate that the resistivity is governed by disorder-induced band broadening in momentum space rather than by local density-of-states effects, providing a unified microscopic interpretation of the breakdown of Linde's rule in Cu-based alloys.
summary: This theoretical study investigates how disorder affects electrical resistivity in Cu alloys doped with 3d metals. By comparing three magnetic models (DLM, FM, NM), the authors find that resistivity scales strongly with the momentum-space broadening of electronic states (BSF FWHM). This establishes a unified picture showing that scattering is governed by band structure broadening rather than just local electron density.
main_problem: To determine the microscopic mechanism governing the resistivity increase in dilute Cu-3d transition-metal alloys at ambient temperatures.
main_result: Resistivity is governed by disorder-induced band broadening (measured via BSF FWHM) in momentum space, rather than solely by local density of states effects. The Double Local Moment (DLM) framework successfully reproduces experimental trends.
method: First-principles calculations using the Korringa–Kohn–Rostoker coherent potential approximation (KKR-CPA) combined with the Kubo–Greenwood formalism to calculate electrical conductivity.
model_or_system: The study investigates dilute solid-solution alloys of Copper (Cu) and 3d transition metals (X). Theoretical models compare Double Local Moment (DLM), Ferromagnetic (FM), and Non-Magnetic (NM) paramagnetic states.
key_observables: Electrical resistivity ($ho$), Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of the Bloch Spectral Function (BSF) on the Fermi surface, Partial Density of States (pDOS) at the Fermi level ($E_F$).
important_parameters: Ambient temperature regime ($T \gg T_K$); solute concentration ($	ext{Cu}_{0.99}	ext{X}_{0.01}$); power-law exponent $ eta \approx 1.89$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the validity of the DLM framework at room temperature, contrasting with low-temperature Kondo regimes; it also notes that pDOS alone is insufficient to explain resistivity variations.
figures_summary: Figures compare $\deltaho$ vs. BSF FWHM (showing strong correlation) and show comparisons between different magnetic states' spectral functions and energy differences used for $T_C$ estimation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares three theoretical descriptions of the paramagnetic state (DLM, FM, NM) using advanced electronic structure calculations to diagnose which physical quantity—pDOS or BSF FWHM—best correlates with measured resistivity trends across the 3d series.
why_interesting: Although focused on solid-state physics, the methodology involves analyzing spectral broadening and scattering rates derived from Green's functions, techniques relevant to understanding decoherence in quantum systems.
